title: Gerunds and infinitives after common verbs
objectives: Choose -ing or a to-infinitive after common verbs.
Distinguish two meanings of stop followed by a verb.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: When one verb follows another, the first verb often determines the form of the second. Some verbs are commonly followed by an -ing form: ‘I enjoy reading’ and ‘She avoided answering’. Other verbs are commonly followed by a to-infinitive: ‘They decided to leave’ and ‘I hope to see you’. A to-infinitive is to plus the base form of a verb.

The -ing form used in patterns such as ‘enjoy reading’ is often called a gerund. It names an activity. The form looks the same as the -ing form in ‘She is reading’, but its role in the sentence is different. Learning the first verb together with its pattern helps you choose the next form.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Common verbs followed by -ing include enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest and mind: ‘We finished eating’ and ‘I suggest taking a taxi’. A negative -ing form can use not before -ing: ‘She suggested not driving’. The subject of the activity depends on context; a different person can also be identified in some more advanced patterns.

Common verbs followed by a to-infinitive include decide, hope, plan, want and promise: ‘They decided to leave’ and ‘I hope to return’. A negative infinitive uses not before to: ‘He decided not to go’. Do not put an extra to after the infinitive marker: ‘plan to visit’, not ‘plan to to visit’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘I enjoy swimming’ with ‘I want to swim’. Both concern swimming, but enjoy and want take different patterns. ‘I enjoy swimming’ says the activity gives me pleasure. ‘I want to swim’ expresses a wish. The pattern belongs to the first verb, so changing that verb can require a different form.

Some verbs allow both forms. Like, love and hate often allow -ing or a to-infinitive in many contexts: ‘I like reading’ and ‘I like to read’. Meaning and context can affect the choice. Other verbs can change meaning with the form that follows: ‘She stopped smoking’ means she stopped the activity, whether temporarily or permanently, while ‘She stopped to smoke’ means she stopped another activity in order to smoke.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use a to-infinitive directly after enjoy in this pattern: ‘enjoy reading’, not ‘enjoy to read’. Do not use an -ing form directly after decide in this pattern: ‘decide to leave’, not ‘decide leaving’. These are verb-specific patterns; do not assume every -ing form or infinitive works after every verb.

Some verbs have additional patterns beyond the ones taught here. Suggest, for example, can be followed by a clause: ‘I suggest that we leave’. This unit practises the common -ing pattern after suggest and does not ask you to memorise every possible structure. In exercises, use the stated verb and context.

examples.note: Enjoy is followed by an -ing form.
Avoid is followed by an -ing form.
Finish is followed by an -ing form.
Decide is followed here by a to-infinitive.

examples.note: Hope is followed by a to-infinitive.

summary: Enjoy, avoid and finish commonly take an -ing form.
Decide, hope, plan and want commonly take a to-infinitive.
Some verbs allow both forms, sometimes with a change in meaning.
